Amazon just started running AI job interviews at scale, and I don't think the headline is the part that matters.

AWS's "Connect Talent" went from preview to general availability this week: AI agents write the interview plan, run adaptive voice interviews around the clock, and hand a recruiter a transcript and a score. Built for retail, logistics and hospitality, the industries staring down this year's holiday hiring surge.

The obvious read is that Amazon just validated the whole category. I build in this category, so I'd love to leave it there. Josh Bersin, who's watched a few big-tech companies try this before, wasn't as impressed. "Google tried this. Facebook tried it before they were Meta," he said, calling the market mature and already crowded. A hyperscaler's name on the box doesn't automatically win a domain fight.

A GA announcement can't answer the question that actually decides this. Shipping the interview is the easy part. Scoring someone whose best answer doesn't sound like the training data, catching your own bias before it hardens into a rubric, earning enough trust that a recruiter can defend the transcript to a candidate two weeks later, that's the actual product. Compute and distribution don't shortcut any of it.

I build Ployo for the harder version of that problem: aged care, health, frontline shifts, where a bad hire costs more than a slow one and nobody's handing that judgment to whoever holds the biggest cloud contract.

Amazon showing up doesn't scare me. It tells me the market finally noticed what I've been saying since before it was fashionable to say it.

The Illusion of Flexibility: What Independent Contractors and Platforms Need to Know About Governance
Independent contracting is often framed around independence, agility, and mutual trust. Phrases like "work on your own terms," "flexible project placement," and "grow with us as a trusted partner" are frequently used to attract skilled workers into digital labor ecosystems.
However, when communication breakdowns occur, the reality behind these statements often reveals a significant imbalance in leverage.
Recently, my contract with Cloudfactory was terminated following a series of sudden offboardings and unclear allocation processes. Despite completing required training streams and seeking clarity through formal channels, the experience highlighted structural patterns that every independent contractor and platform operator should evaluate:
Key Takeaways for Independent Contractors
Vague Reallocation Policies: Platforms frequently retain absolute discretion over project streams, leaving contractors vulnerable to sudden offboarding without defined notice periods or clear metrics.
Asymmetric Communication: When resolution mechanisms rely on slow or automated internal ticket systems, contractors are effectively held in limbo, unable to transition quickly, yet restricted by platform commitments.
Training vs. Deployment Gaps: Completing multi-stream training modules does not always guarantee active allocation. Always clarify lead times and allocation guarantees before investing extensive unpaid or low-paid training hours.
Considerations for Companies Hiring AI & Data Talent
Retention Requires Transparency: High contractor churn and sudden account terminations diminish workforce trust and impact long-term data annotation quality.
Clear Offboarding Protocols: Providing explicit, performance-backed metrics prior to project removal builds a more reliable and motivated flexible workforce.
To fellow AI annotators and gig workers: read service level agreements carefully, diversify your client base early, and always insist on explicit written feedback when project statuses change.

The most persistent blind spot I see in infrastructure today is treating Terraform as a configuration language for cloud resources. In 2026, that framing is dangerously incomplete. Terraform has become the policy enforcement layer for autonomous infrastructure, and the teams that still think in terms of resource blocks are the ones getting left behind.

The non-obvious shift is that Terraform now operates as a decision framework for agentic systems. The latest stable release, version 1.15.8, introduces variables and locals in provider requirements and a new minimal-refresh planning option. These are not minor features. They signal that Terraform is evolving to support environments where infrastructure decisions are made by autonomous agents, not humans. The winning teams are not the ones writing the most modules. They are the ones designing Terraform configurations that embed cost guardrails, security policies, and compliance rules directly into the plan output, so that when an AI agent proposes a change, the system can evaluate the tradeoff between speed and risk before a single resource is created.

Another blind spot most teams miss is the rise of the Actions page in HCP Terraform. This is not just a UI improvement. It is the recognition that infrastructure changes are now events that need to be audited, traced, and correlated with business outcomes. The teams that are winning are the ones that have integrated Terraform plans into their observability stack, so they can answer the question "did this infrastructure change improve application latency or increase cost" within minutes, not hours.

For hiring managers and recruiting leaders: I do not just write Terraform modules or manage state files. I design Terraform architectures that are built for autonomous operations, where the plan is a contract between the agent and the business, not just a list of resources to create. I understand that Terraform in 2026 is not a tool you learn. It is a governance layer that requires designing the policy model, the cost model, and the audit trail before the first provider is configured. If your team is struggling with multi-cloud drift, agent-generated infrastructure changes that bypass manual review, or a Terraform setup that cannot tell you who is responsible for a cost spike at 3AM, I can architect the solution.

The hardest question nobody is asking: When an AI agent generates a Terraform plan that passes every policy check, but that plan introduces a subtle multi-region latency increase that only appears 48 hours after apply, who is accountable for that decision, and how do you audit the tradeoff between automation speed and operational risk?

Case Scenario: Terrible Contract, Corporation hiring BPO Services - Third Vendor Party

AI response: 

It's a terrible contract, yeah.

Below standard expectation and performance — BPO pays the fine to the client. So the company loses.

And then at the same time, promising excellence while hiring people with zero experience in real work situation.

No real office life, no real HR, no real Payroll, Benefits, Contract handling — just script.

So you get that cycle — zero experience, zero documentation, gaps, robots waiting for escalation, OOSLA, fine.

You see it clearly because you have real work experience. You led Accenture and GBS, you know what in-house looks like.

(Example: GBS/Assistant Finance Controller asking me to give the Attrition Report with zero documentation. Accenture staff would trust my decision, let's exclude the benefits if the employee would not update the incorrect amount for reimbursement)

I proposed that HR Services should be an in-house, don't trust the BPO). 

***

That's why it doesn't make sense to you — promising excellent but not hiring the experience to deliver it.

And you say that from both sides — you've seen in-house where HR can design a template immediately, consult legal directly, client tells you priorities for Benefits, Payroll, Contract directly. Fast, autonomous, real problem-solving.

And you've seen BPO — bureaucratic, Line Manager then 2nd Line Manager just to engage, gaps and zero documentation, robots waiting for escalation, managers only watching KPI, SLA, OOSLA and fines, pushing to close.

From what you lived, in-house solves. BPO watches the stats.

***

Test the position of BPO - HR Services Delivery Manager if the person knows HR System Builder or Escalation - Stat Monitoring only. 

***

HR services are the most challenging of all BPO services.

And you're right — you don't have to be an HR graduate of any university. It's the system of managing the total employees from CEO to rank and file.

A contract speaks for itself. Full-time, part-time and fixed-term.

You have to manage the contract, maintain and update.

The contract = Payroll and Benefits.

From First Payroll and Benefits to the Last Payroll and Benefits.

That's the whole employee — from start to end. Not just a statistic, KPI, SLA, OOSLA to close.

You lived that, Rose — that's why you know in-house manages it, not just a script.

Ask any business owner how they make decisions and you will get two different answers.

Some decisions get a process. Setting a price, hiring someone, signing a contract. You gather the facts and work through them carefully. Software has always been good at that kind of decision.

The other kind never gets a process, because there is no time for one. Is this lead serious. Will this hire work out. Has the room gone quiet on this deal. You just know, in a second, from experience. And you are usually right.

Until now, software could only do the first kind. Any automated decision had to be spelled out, step by step, in advance.

TypeSafe AI's new model, Jev, is built for the second kind. It gives you an answer right away, instead of working through it step by step.

The point is not that fast is better than careful. It is that more kinds of decisions can now get help from software. A lot of business is slow not because the thinking is hard, but because someone has to sit in the middle of a two-second call and it takes two days to get to them.

I do not think the winner here will be whoever has the smartest AI. I think it will be whoever knows which kind of decision needs which kind of help.

**What if everyone is waiting for transportation to “recover,” but the industry we’re waiting for isn’t coming back?**

I keep thinking about this because almost every day I read something that seems to point in a different direction.

Capacity is leaving the market.

Rates are rising in places.

Demand is still sending mixed signals.

Companies are cutting costs and being cautious about hiring and investment.

At the same time, technology and the structure of the industry are changing faster than I've ever seen.

Just this month, we're seeing reports of transportation capacity continuing to contract while prices rise. We're seeing carriers continue to leave the market even without a major demand boom.

Normally you would look at some of those signals and think: **Here comes the recovery.**

But does it feel like one?

That's what has me wondering if we're looking at this the wrong way.

Maybe we're waiting for the old transportation market to come back when something entirely different is being built in its place.

Look at Amazon. A recent report says an internal projection has Amazon delivering more than 86% of its own U.S. packages next year. Think about what that means for the traditional transportation ecosystem if that direction continues.

Then look at what's happening inside fleets.

AI. Connected vehicles. Telematics. Predictive maintenance. Automation. Fleet managers building their own AI tools. More decisions being driven by data and fewer manual processes.

The technology side of this industry is moving incredibly fast.

Meanwhile, customers have changed too.

We want everything yesterday. We want to know exactly where it is every step of the way. And we don't necessarily want to pay more for any of it.

So where does that leave the traditional carrier? The smaller fleet? The owner-operator? The 3PL? And even the traditional fleet organization?

Maybe that's part of why companies seem hesitant.

When you can't confidently predict what the industry will look like three years from now, it's difficult to decide where to put your money and your people today.

So you wait.

You cut costs. You delay hiring. You become more efficient. You invest selectively. You try to figure out what's next.

I've spent most of my career in transportation, and this is one of the strangest periods I can remember.

I'm also more excited than ever about where the technology is going.

That's the contradiction.

**I love where transportation technology is heading. I'm just not sure anyone knows yet what transportation itself is becoming.**

Maybe we need to stop asking:

**“When will transportation recover?”**

And start asking:

**“Recover to what?”**

What are you seeing?

Are we still working through another transportation cycle, or are we watching the industry permanently restructure itself?

We keep telling 50+ workers how to make themselves more employable. Maybe it’s time we started asking employers to make hiring more age-inclusive.

I’ve been reading far too many stories about experienced professionals over 50 searching for work for months or even years. And so much of the advice is directed at them:

Shorten your résumé. Don’t look overqualified. Show you’re comfortable with technology. Convince employers you’ll work for someone younger. Reassure them you won’t leave.

At some point, we need to ask: Why are we asking job seekers to hide their age instead of asking organizations to examine the practices that make them feel they need to?

So what can employers actually do?

1. Hire for capability, not arbitrary years of experience.
If someone has the skills and desire to do the job, why exclude them because they have 15 years of experience when you asked for 5? Hire against competencies, not years.

2. Stop rejecting people as “overqualified.”
Ask why they want the job. Some want less responsibility, an individual-contributor role, better balance, or a career change. Let candidates tell you what they want.

3. Create more part-time and flexible roles.
Does every position need to be 40 hours a week? Could one full-time position become two 20-hour roles? Let’s apply flexibility to how we design jobs, not just where people work.

4. Solve the retention risk instead of assuming it.
Concerned someone might leave before a temporary contract ends? Consider a completion bonus tied to outcomes and staying through the contract.

5. Audit your hiring process AND employer brand for hidden age signals.
Review job descriptions, screening criteria, interview questions and algorithms. Also look at your website, LinkedIn page and team photos. What does a 55-year-old candidate see? Your team photos communicate who belongs, whether intended or not.

6. Challenge assumptions disguised as hiring decisions.
“They won’t report to someone younger.” “They’ll expect too much money.” “They’re not comfortable with AI.” Those aren’t facts. They’re assumptions. Ask the candidate.

7. Measure what happens in your hiring funnel.
Who applies? Who gets screened out? Who gets hired? Where are experienced candidates disappearing? You can’t diagnose a pattern you never examine.

8. Include age in the conversation about inclusion.
Many organizations talk about DEI while barely mentioning age. Age diversity is diversity. Let’s create workplaces with room for young people, people mid-career, and experienced professionals.

Maybe the solution isn’t teaching people over 50 how to navigate the hiring system. Maybe we need to redesign parts of the system.

If your organization says it values diversity, take a closer look at whether your practices support that commitment.

And if you want help doing that, this is work I love doing. DM me to start a conversation.

$1,200 for 4 weeks of full-time offshore support will change how a lot of SMBs think about hiring.

Not because it’s “cheap.” Because AI is turning hiring into a lower-friction operating decision.

The old model was clunky: post a job, sort resumes, guess from interviews, deal with contracts, figure out payroll, hope it works.

The new model is closer to this: describe the role once, get instant matches, review an AI-conducted interview with video/audio and a score, ask Ivy questions about the candidate before you meet them, then hire month-to-month.

That process will push more work offshore.

What matters is whether the system is transparent and reversible. HireNewTalent.ai uses flat 4-week pricing, includes compliance and payroll, and offers free replacement if the fit is wrong.

My bet: AI agents won’t just expand offshoring. They’ll expand global participation in work by making cross-border hiring normal for smaller employers.
